title: What Cursor and OpenAI's rev-per-employee numbers really tell you
linkedinPost:
Cursor: $3.3M revenue per employee. Or $40M. Depends who you ask.

Both numbers are real.

The $3.3M uses a 300-person headcount and ARR run-rate. The $40M uses a 50-engineer headcount and the same ARR run-rate during hypergrowth.

Same company. Same revenue. Different denominator. Different methodology.

Most financial services firms see these benchmarks and make one of 3 mistakes:

• They compare Cursor's run-rate ARR against their own GAAP revenue — not the same thing
• They ignore that Cursor has no AML officer, no compliance team, no risk function at scale — because they're not a regulated entity
• They set an RPE target without identifying which workflows to automate — which produces headcount pressure, not architectural change

Klarna is the comparison that actually transfers. Revenue per employee up 73% in one year — not by becoming AI-native, but by automating specific, named workflows: customer service interactions, code generation, document processing.

That path is legible. Identifiable workflows. Measurable throughput gains. EU-compliant from the start.

What I would actually do:

• Run a Revenue Density Audit by function — not company-wide
• Target the 5 highest-volume, most deterministic workflows first: KYC document extraction, transaction monitoring triage, credit memo drafts
• Wire EU AI Act Article 12 logging before the first agentic deployment
• Report RPE by function quarterly, not company-wide annually
• Don't set an RPE target — set an automation target, and let RPE follow

Revenue per employee is an outcome. The workflows you automate are the lever.

Full piece + the Revenue Density Audit I use with clients — link in comments.

@graph.headline: What Cursor and OpenAI's rev-per-employee numbers really tell you
@graph.description: Cursor's $3.3M–$40M revenue per employee is real — and widely misread. Here is what the benchmark actually signals for regulated financial services operators.

mainEntity.name: What is AI-native revenue per employee?

acceptedAnswer.text: AI-native revenue per employee measures annual revenue generated per full-time employee at companies built from founding on AI-powered processes. It differs from the same metric at traditional companies because AI-native firms operate with dramatically smaller teams relative to revenue — often $1M–$40M per employee versus $100K–$400K at conventional organisations.

mainEntity.name: Why is Cursor's revenue per employee so high compared to other companies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cursor's RPE is exceptionally high for 2 reasons: it is a product-led growth business with minimal sales headcount, and the most-cited figures use a small early headcount (50 engineers) against a run-rate ARR figure during hypergrowth. Figures using the full 300-employee headcount put Cursor at $3.3M per employee — still exceptional, but a different order of magnitude. The more useful observation is that Cursor was built AI-native from founding, which kept headcount low even as revenue compounded.

mainEntity.name: Can a bank or regulated financial services firm achieve AI-native revenue per employee levels?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not directly. Regulated institutions carry compliance, risk, legal, and audit headcount that AI-native startups do not. The achievable goal is moving from $200–400K per employee toward $600K–$1M — the Klarna trajectory — by automating high-volume deterministic workflows in ops and customer service. That is a 2–4x RPE improvement over 3–5 years, which is commercially significant.

mainEntity.name: How do I start measuring revenue per employee by function in my organisation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Begin by mapping revenue attribution: which functions contribute directly to revenue, which enable it, which are regulatory obligations. Divide each function's attributed revenue by headcount. Run this quarterly. The function with the highest volume, most deterministic work, and lowest current RPE is your first AI automation target. Start there — not with the most exciting use case.
